title: Al-Ghazali's crisis
hookLine: the well-known scholar leaves his post in doubt and finds the living path (Deliverance from Error)

lines: AT THE TOP OF HIS FIELD.
HE STANDS TO TEACH, AND CAN'T.
cards: A professor at the top of his field. Students crowding his lectures, rulers asking his opinion, his books read everywhere. One day he stands up to teach, and can't speak.
His tongue won't move. He can't eat. The doctors examine him and say it isn't his body; it's something in his heart.
That happened in Baghdad, in the year 1095, to a celebrated scholar. He wrote about it himself, later, in a short book about his search for certainty.

teach.b: His name was Abu Hamid al-Ghazali, a master of law, theology and philosophy, and he taught at the Nizamiyya, the great college of Baghdad.
In his book, Deliverance from Error, he says he'd started doubting how anyone can know anything for certain.

He went through every school he could find: the theologians, the philosophers, the ones who claimed secret teachers. Finally he turned to the Sufis, read their books, and understood them. Then it hit him.

teach.h: HE COULD EXPLAIN IT, NOT WALK IT.
teach.b: He could explain their path perfectly, and he hadn't walked a single step of it. Knowing the definition of health, he says, isn't being healthy; knowing what makes a person full isn't being full.

The Sufi word for the second kind of knowing is dhawq, tasting. As if he could describe honey without ever tasting it. And he saw that his fame, his salary and his reputation were the very things holding him back.

teach.h: HE GAVE IT UP AND LEFT.
teach.b: So he gave away his wealth, except what his family needed, and left Baghdad quietly. For years he traveled, to Damascus, Jerusalem and the holy cities, praying, keeping silent, practicing.
In those years he wrote his great work, the Revival of the Religious Sciences, joining the law and the inner path in one book. Later Muslims called him Hujjat al-Islam, the proof of Islam.
It started with admitting a doubt.

how: Al-Ghazali's Revival of the Religious Sciences is still read in mosques and study circles, and his account of his crisis is often taught as a model of honest searching within the faith.

games.q: you're a celebrated scholar in Baghdad. you can explain the Sufi path perfectly, but you've never walked it, and now you can't speak. what do you do?
o: rest a while, then return to lecturing.
give away your wealth and leave to practice what you know.
write a book refuting the Sufis.
games.why: he gave away his wealth, left Baghdad quietly, and spent years in prayer and practice, then wrote the Revival.

practice: Think of something you're supposed to be sure of, about faith, your work, a relationship or yourself, and notice honestly where you're unsure.

Don't solve it and don't panic; al-Ghazali's doubt was the door, not the end, so just name it plainly to yourself. If you pray, bring the doubt to God as it is; if you don't, let it sit beside you without arguing.

wordCard.voice: Al-Ghazali's crisis. The great scholar who lost his voice, left his post, and went looking to taste what he knew. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: taste, tasting; in Sufi writing, knowing by direct experience.

carryVoice: Your line: knowing is not tasting. Honey has to reach the tongue. See you tomorrow.
